learn.hook: Riding a bicycle, fearing the dentist's chair, typing on a phone keyboard without looking: none of these came pre-installed. You learnt them. But is every change in behaviour learning?
points: Learning is a key process through which behaviour changes as a result of experience; much of what we do is learnt.
Definition: learning is any relatively permanent change in behaviour or behavioural potential produced by experience or practice.
Changes due to maturation (e.g. a baby starting to walk), fatigue, drugs, illness or injury are NOT learning, because they don't come from experience/practice or are not relatively permanent.
Features: learning always involves experience; the changes are relatively permanent; learning cannot be seen directly, so it is inferred from performance.
Learning is a process with a sequence of psychological events, e.g. measuring performance before (pre-test), practising, and measuring after (post-test) to see the change.

example.q: Which of these is learning? (a) Sleepy after a heavy lunch you type slowly. (b) After months of practice you type 60 words per minute. (c) A child's voice deepens at puberty.
steps: (a) Temporary change due to fatigue → not learning.
(b) Relatively permanent change from practice → learning.
(c) Change due to maturation → not learning.

learn.reallife: Indian Railways loco pilots train for months in simulators before driving real trains; their improved, lasting performance after practice is learning, while a bad day due to tiredness is not.

topics.title: Paradigms of learning and Pavlov's experiment

learn.hook: In the 1900s, Russian physiologist Ivan Pavlov was studying digestion in dogs when he noticed something odd: the dogs started drooling before the food arrived, at the sound of footsteps. That accident opened up a whole field.
points: Types (paradigms) of learning: classical conditioning, operant (instrumental) conditioning, observational learning, cognitive learning, verbal learning and skill learning.
The simplest kind of learning is conditioning, which is associative learning: learning that two events go together.
Pavlov's experiment: a dog was harnessed and its saliva measured through a tube. A bell was sounded and food was given just after. After several pairings, the bell alone made the dog salivate.
So the dog learnt an association between the bell and food: this is classical conditioning.

example.q: Describe Pavlov's procedure in three phases.
steps: Before conditioning: food → salivation; bell → no salivation.
During conditioning: bell is sounded and then food is given, repeatedly.
After conditioning: bell alone → salivation.
example.answer: Bell paired repeatedly with food until the bell alone produced salivation.

learn.reallife: Hear the ting of a Swiggy or Zomato notification and your stomach rumbles? The sound has been paired with food so often that it alone triggers hunger signals, a modern Pavlovian effect.

topics.title: US, UR, CS and CR: acquisition of conditioned responses

learn.hook: A child gets an injection and cries. Next visit, she cries the moment she sees the white coat. Psychologists can label every part of that sad little chain.
points: Unconditioned stimulus (US): naturally produces a response without learning (food). Unconditioned response (UR): the natural, unlearned response to the US (salivation to food).

Conditioned stimulus (CS): an originally neutral stimulus that, after pairing with the US, produces a response (bell). Conditioned response (CR): the learned response to the CS (salivation to the bell).
Acquisition: the CR is acquired through repeated pairings of the CS with the US; the CS must reliably predict the US.
Everyday examples: fear of a dentist's drill sound, liking a song linked to happy times, feeling hungry at the sight of a restaurant logo.

example.q: A child is stung by a bee (pain, crying). Later, the buzzing sound alone makes her afraid. Label US, UR, CS and CR.
steps: Bee sting naturally causes pain/fear → US.
Fear/crying to the sting → UR.
Buzzing sound, originally neutral, paired with the sting → CS.
Fear to the buzzing alone → CR.
example.answer: US = sting; UR = fear to sting; CS = buzzing; CR = fear to buzzing

learn.reallife: Many people feel anxious at the sound of an exam-hall bell years after school: the bell (CS) was repeatedly paired with high-stakes tests (US).

learn.hook: Ring the bell after the food, and Pavlov's dogs barely learn anything. Ring it just before, and they learn fast. Timing is everything in classical conditioning.
points: Time relations between CS and US: simultaneous (CS and US begin together), delayed (CS begins first and stays on until the US begins), trace (CS begins and ends before the US begins, leaving a memory trace), backward (US is presented before the CS).
Delayed conditioning is the most effective; backward conditioning is the least effective (learning is rare).

Type of US: appetitive US (pleasant, e.g. food, water) produces approach responses; aversive US (painful or harmful, e.g. shock, loud noise) produces avoidance or escape responses. Aversive conditioning is often established very quickly, sometimes in one trial.
Intensity of the CS: a more intense CS leads to faster acquisition, i.e. fewer trials are needed.

example.q: A light (CS) comes on and stays on; after 2 seconds food (US) arrives, and the light goes off. In another set-up, the light flashes for 1 second and goes off, then food comes 5 seconds later. Name both procedures.
steps: Set-up 1: CS starts first and overlaps until the US begins → delayed conditioning.
Set-up 2: CS ends before the US starts, a gap is left → trace conditioning.

topics.title: Operant conditioning: Skinner and the Skinner box

learn.hook: A hungry rat in a box presses a lever by accident; a food pellet drops. It presses again. Soon it's pressing like a pro. B.F. Skinner turned this simple scene into one of psychology's biggest ideas.
points: Operant conditioning was first investigated by B.F. Skinner. Operants are voluntary behaviours that 'operate' on the environment; they are controlled by their consequences.
Skinner box: a hungry rat placed in a box with a lever. When it presses the lever, a food pellet is delivered. Over trials, lever pressing increases.
It is also called instrumental conditioning because the response is instrumental (the means) in getting the reward.
Reinforcement is any stimulus or event that increases the probability of the response it follows; it strengthens the response.

example.q: Explain the Skinner box experiment in terms of response, consequence and learning.
steps: Response: the rat presses the lever (a voluntary operant).
Consequence: food pellet (reinforcer) follows.
Learning: the probability of lever pressing increases with repeated reinforcement.
example.answer: The lever press (operant) is strengthened because it is followed by food (reinforcement).

learn.reallife: Loyalty programmes from airlines or supermarkets reward you with points every time you buy; your buying behaviour (operant) gets reinforced by consequences.

topics.title: Reinforcers: positive, negative, primary and secondary

learn.hook: You take a painkiller, the headache vanishes, and next time you reach for the same tablet faster. Nothing pleasant was given; something unpleasant was removed. That still counts as reinforcement.
points: Positive reinforcers: pleasant consequences (food, money, praise) whose presentation strengthens a response. Negative reinforcers: unpleasant or painful stimuli (noise, pain, cold); a response that removes, escapes or avoids them is strengthened (negative reinforcement).
Primary reinforcers are biological and unlearned (food, water, relief from pain); secondary reinforcers acquire value through association with primary ones (money, grades, praise, medals).
Number, amount and quality of reinforcement matter: more reinforced trials, a larger amount and a higher-quality reward generally lead to faster learning (up to a point).
Delay of reinforcement: the longer the delay between response and reinforcer, the slower and weaker the learning; immediate reinforcement works best.

example.q: Classify: (a) A child gets chocolate for finishing homework. (b) Fastening the seatbelt stops the car's annoying beep, so you buckle up sooner each time. (c) Money for good marks.
steps: (a) Pleasant consequence added → positive reinforcement; chocolate is a primary reinforcer.
(b) Unpleasant beep removed → negative reinforcement.

learn.hook: Why do people keep scratching lottery tickets, refreshing social media, or calling a busy friend again and again? The secret is not how much they are rewarded, but on what schedule.
points: Continuous reinforcement: every correct response is reinforced. Partial (intermittent) reinforcement: only some responses are reinforced.

Fixed ratio (FR): reinforcement after a fixed number of responses (e.g. paid per 10 shirts stitched). Variable ratio (VR): after a varying, unpredictable number of responses (e.g. lottery, slot machines).

Fixed interval (FI): reinforcement for the first response after a fixed time period (e.g. monthly salary, a weekly test). Variable interval (VI): for the first response after varying time periods (e.g. surprise quizzes, checking for a message).

Partial reinforcement produces greater resistance to extinction than continuous reinforcement: responses learned with partial reinforcement last longer when rewards stop. Variable schedules produce the most persistent responding.
Continuous reinforcement is best for fast initial learning; partial reinforcement is best for maintaining a behaviour.

(b) Reward available after unpredictable time periods → variable interval.
(c) Reward after an unpredictable number of responses → variable ratio.

topics.title: Punishment, negative reinforcement, escape and avoidance

learn.hook: Board exam favourite: 'Negative reinforcement is a kind of punishment.' True or false? False, and examiners love that trap. Let's make sure you never fall into it.
points: Punishment: an aversive stimulus following a response, which decreases (weakens or suppresses) that response, e.g. a fine for littering.

Negative reinforcement: removal of an aversive stimulus following a response, which increases (strengthens) that response, e.g. taking a painkiller that removes a headache. So negative reinforcement is NOT punishment.
Escape conditioning: learning a response that ends an aversive situation that is already present (e.g. leaving a smoky room, opening an umbrella in the rain).
Avoidance conditioning: learning a response that prevents an aversive situation before it begins (e.g. leaving home early to avoid a traffic jam, carrying an umbrella when clouds gather).

example.q: Classify: (a) A student who talks in class has to stay back after school, and talks less. (b) Wearing earplugs stops the irritating construction noise, and you wear them more often. (c) Leaving for the station early to avoid missing the train.
steps: (a) Aversive consequence decreases the behaviour → punishment.
(b) Aversive noise removed, behaviour increases → negative reinforcement (escape).
(c) Response prevents the aversive event → avoidance conditioning.

topics.title: Key learning processes: extinction, recovery, generalisation, discrimination, shaping

learn.hook: A puppy bitten by a large black dog starts fearing all black dogs, then all dogs. A circus elephant learns a complex trick one tiny step at a time. Same learning principles, different directions.
points: Extinction: the weakening and eventual disappearance of a learned response when reinforcement (or the US) is no longer given, e.g. the bell repeatedly sounded without food.
Spontaneous recovery: after extinction and a rest period, the extinguished response reappears when the CS is presented again (usually weaker).

Generalisation: responding in the same way to stimuli similar to the original CS (fear of one dog → fear of similar dogs). Discrimination: responding differently to different stimuli, e.g. responding only to the reinforced tone, not similar tones.
Shaping: reinforcing successive approximations, small steps closer and closer to the desired behaviour, until the complex behaviour is learned.
Chaining: linking a series of simple responses into a complex sequence, each step leading to the next (e.g. a dance routine).

topics.title: Observational learning: Bandura's Bobo doll study

learn.hook: Nobody gives a toddler a reward for holding a phone to her ear and saying 'Hello?'. She just watched you. Much of what we learn, we learn by watching.
points: Observational learning (also called modelling or social learning): learning by observing the behaviour of others (models) and its consequences.
Bandura's Bobo doll experiment: children watched a film in which an adult hit and kicked an inflatable Bobo doll. In different versions, the model was rewarded, punished, or received no consequences.

Afterwards, children who saw the model punished showed the least aggression; but when all children were offered rewards to imitate, they all showed aggressive acts, proving that they had learned the behaviour by watching even if they had not performed it.
Observational learning explains socialisation (learning social norms and manners), fashion trends and many social skills, and also how violent media can teach aggression.

example.q: In Bandura's study, why did children who saw the model punished still hit the doll when offered rewards?
steps: Watching the model punished reduced their performance of aggression.

example.answer: They had learned the behaviour through observation; punishment of the model only suppressed performance.

topics.title: Cognitive learning: insight and latent learning

learn.hook: You've been stuck on a geometry proof for twenty minutes, and then suddenly, 'Aha!' the whole solution clicks. That flash is the heart of cognitive learning.
points: Cognitive learning involves changes in what the learner knows (understanding, mental representations) rather than just in behaviour.

Insight learning (Wolfgang Kohler): chimpanzees (such as Sultan) placed in a cage with bananas out of reach first tried and failed, then paused and suddenly solved the problem, e.g. by joining two sticks or stacking boxes. Insight is sudden, and the solution is remembered and transferred to similar problems.

Latent learning (Edward Tolman): rats allowed to explore a maze without any reward later found the food quickly once a reward was introduced. They had formed a cognitive map (a mental representation of the layout), and learning stayed hidden (latent) until there was a reason to show it.
Insight vs latent: insight = sudden solution after a period of problem-solving; latent = learning without reinforcement that is not shown until needed.

example.q: Raghav cycles around his new neighbourhood with no particular goal. A month later, when a road is blocked, he immediately takes a detour he has never used. Which type of learning?

It appeared only when there was a need.
He had formed a cognitive map → latent learning (Tolman).

learn.hook: Memorising Hindi-English word pairs, the periodic table in order, or a shopping list in any order: each uses a different verbal-learning method that psychologists have studied since the 1880s.
points: Verbal learning: learning words and verbal material. Hermann Ebbinghaus pioneered it using nonsense syllables (e.g. consonant-vowel-consonant 'trigrams' like 'BEM', 'DIK') to avoid the influence of meaning.
Paired-associates learning: learning pairs, where the first word is the stimulus term and the second the response term, e.g. learning foreign-language words with their meanings.

Serial learning: learning items in a fixed order (e.g. planets from the Sun, steps of a procedure). Free recall: recalling items in any order; items at the beginning and end of a list are usually recalled better than those in the middle.

Determinants: length of list (longer → more trials needed), meaningfulness of material (meaningful material is learned faster), and how often items have been used (frequency). Organisation helps: clustering (recalling words in categories) and subjective organisation (the learner's own grouping of unrelated words).

example.q: Classify the method: (a) Learning 'chhatri - umbrella, kitaab - book'. (b) Learning the order of the planets. (c) Recalling 20 random words in any order you like.
steps: (a) Pairs with stimulus and response terms → paired-associates.
(b) Fixed order → serial learning.
(c) Any order → free recall.

topics.title: Skill learning and factors that facilitate learning

learn.hook: Your first day of driving: mirror, clutch, gear, indicator, panic. A year later you drive while chatting about cricket. Skills go through predictable phases.
points: A skill is the ability to perform a complex task smoothly and efficiently; it involves a sequence of perceptual-motor responses (e.g. driving, typing, playing the tabla).

Fitts's three phases of skill learning: cognitive (understanding instructions, many errors, full attention), associative (errors reduce, steps get linked, performance improves) and autonomous (performance becomes automatic and needs little attention).
Practice, with feedback about performance, is essential for skill learning: skills improve with practice, and knowing results helps correct errors.
Motivation facilitates learning: intrinsic motivation (learning for its own sake, interest, enjoyment) and extrinsic motivation (learning for external rewards like marks or prizes).
Preparedness: species differ in their biological readiness to learn certain associations; some are learned very easily (e.g. linking taste with sickness), others with difficulty.

example.q: Identify the phase: (a) A new typist looks at the keys and makes many errors. (b) She types faster with fewer mistakes, though still with effort. (c) She types while talking, without looking.
steps: (a) Understanding and many errors → cognitive phase.
(b) Fewer errors, steps linked → associative phase.
(c) Automatic, little attention → autonomous phase.

learn.hook: Taare Zameen Par made millions of Indians aware that a bright child who mixes up 'b' and 'd' is not lazy or stupid. He may have a learning disability, and with the right teaching he can thrive.
points: A learning disability is a general term for difficulties in acquiring and using reading, writing, speaking, listening, reasoning and mathematical skills, in people whose intelligence is normal. It is thought to arise from differences in how the brain processes information.

Common signs: difficulty in writing letters, words and phrases, in reading text aloud and in speaking; confusing similar letters (b/d, p/q) or reading 'was' as 'saw'; poor listening skills; attention problems; poor sense of time and space; poor motor coordination; poor learning strategies.

Dyslexia (difficulty in reading and spelling) is one of the most common forms. Learning disabilities are NOT due to intellectual disability, sensory impairment (e.g. poor eyesight) or lack of educational opportunity.
Early identification and remedial teaching (special methods suited to the child, often multi-sensory) help children with learning disabilities learn effectively; support at home and school matters.

example.q: Ishaan, aged 9, is good at drawing and solving puzzles but reverses letters while writing, struggles to read aloud and often loses track of time. His eyesight and hearing are normal. What might be the issue, and what should be done?

He should be assessed by a professional and given remedial teaching, with patient support.
